en: The Sūtra on Impermanence. Om, homage to the All-Knowing One!
1. Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery, together with a great saṅgha of twelve hundred and fifty monks.
2. Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the monks:
"Monks, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, unreliable, and subject to change.
Therefore, monks, it is enough to feel revulsion toward all conditioned phenomena; it is enough to become dispassionate toward them; it is enough to be liberated from them."
3. For all beings, for all creatures, for all living things, life indeed lasts until the end of death; it culminates in death. There is no non-death for one who is born.

4. Furthermore, those householders who were from great *sāla*-tree clans, great *brāhmaṇa* clans, or great *kṣatriya* clans—possessing vast wealth and great enjoyments; with abundant jewels, gold coins, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, gold, silver, and various articles of property;

with abundant stores of money, grain, and granaries; with abundant female and male slaves, laborers, and servants; and with abundant friends, ministers, kinsmen, and blood relations—[all these, having heard this Dharma discourse, will likewise attain supreme perfect enlightenment].
For them too, life ends in death; it culminates in death. There is no immortality for one who is born.

5. Furthermore, O monks, even those kings who are Kṣatriyas consecrated by coronation, who have attained sovereignty, power, and prowess over the provinces, and who dwell having conquered a great circle of the earth—even for them life ends in death; it terminates in death, for there is no non-death for one who is born.

(As 32) Even those monks who are seers living as forest-dwellers, subsisting on wild fruits, eating wild fruits, and maintaining themselves with wild fruits—even for them life ends in death; death is the finality of existence; there is no non-death for one who is born.

7. Moreover, O monks, even for those gods of the desire realm—the gods of the Four Great Kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods—their life ends in death;
death is its final conclusion. For there is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.
8. Furthermore, those material gods who have attained the first dhyāna—the Brahmakāyikas, Brahmapurohitas, Brahmapārṣadyas, and Mahābrahmans;
and those who have attained the second dhyāna—the Parīttaśubhas, Apramāṇaśubhas, and Ābhāsvaras—

The gods who have attained the third dhyāna are the Parīttaśubhas, the Apramāṇaśubhas, and the Śubhakṛtsnas; those who have attained the fourth dhyāna are the Anabhrakas, the Puṇyaprasavas, the Bṛhatphalas, the Asaṃjñisattvas, the Avṛhas (As 33), the Atapas, the Sudarśas, the Sudarśanas, and the Akaniṣṭhas.
For even their life ends in death; death is its final conclusion. There is no such thing as non-death for one who is born.

9. Furthermore, those monks who are formless gods—those who have reached the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—even for them life ends in death; death is the finality of existence. For one who is born, there is no non-death. This is the triple world.

10. Furthermore, those monks who are arhats— whose taints are exhausted, who have accomplished their task, completed what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, whose minds are rightly liberated through perfect knowledge, and who have reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states— even for them, the body is subject to being cast off.

11. Furthermore, monks, even those Pratyekabuddhas who are like the rhinoceros horn, who tame themselves alone, who pacify themselves alone, and who bring themselves alone to final nirvana—even for them, this body is subject to being laid down.

12. Furthermore, those monks, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, who possess the power of the ten powers, who are noble bulls, who roar the true lion’s roar, and who possess the four grounds of self-confidence:

the ground of self-confidence in ascending the Dharma, the ground of self-confidence in teaching all Dharmas, the ground of self-confidence in leading others to enter the path to Nirvāṇa, and the ground of self-confidence in the knowledge that has abandoned the outflows;
whose bodies are firm, solid, and like those of Nārāyaṇa—(As 34)
Even for them, this body is subject to being cast aside.

13. "Monks, just as vessels made by a potter—whether unbaked or baked—are destined for breaking and end in breaking, even so, monks, for all beings, for all creatures, for all living things, life ends in death and terminates in death; there is no non-death for one who is born."
The Blessed One said this;
having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke:
"Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to the nature of arising and passing away."
For having arisen, they indeed cease; their subsiding is happiness.
Just as a vessel made of clay by a potter ends inevitably in breaking, so too is the life of sentient beings.
Just as ripe fruits are constantly in fear of falling,
so too are sentient beings born of conditioned formations always in fear of death.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation; for life indeed ends in death.
(As 35) 15. Thus spoke the Blessed One; and those monks and those assemblies, with uplifted minds, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
Thus ends the Noble Sūtra on Impermanence.
All the verses used here are found in the Udānavarga (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden X, edited by F. Bernhard, Vol. I, Göttingen 1965), in the Anityavarga.
Verses 3, 12, 11, and 22.
